Original: Food webs are invaluable to understanding the organisation of natural communities and their response to climate disturbances, but their construction is inherently resource intensive and often lead to incomplete sampling and excessive processing. Machine learning has emerged as a potential tool to identifying missing links in empirical food webs; however, their application is currently restricted to predicting a small number of links, or lacks ecological realism. Patterns embedded in network substructures form highly informative learning features when predicting links in social and other complex networks, but their suitability for ecology is yet to be explored. Here, we extended the Weisfeiler-Lehman Neural Machine, which harnesses substructural patterns by encoding nodes based on their organisational roles, to infer trophic links in food webs by preserving the resource to consumer direction of energy transfer and generating negative samples through negative sampling based on trophic roles with hybrid top-up. We evaluated our approach using 290 food webs from across the globe, and found that our method is able to capture missing links with minimal false predictions. Moreover, our approach enables the construction of whole food webs accurately with as little as 60% of the trophic links , with the pseudo food webs exhibiting comparable network properties as the empirical food webs. The rapidly changing climate calls for more innovative and rapid bioassessment, and our approach paves the way for accelerating and simplifying sampling efforts in current biomonitoring regime.

Original: Here, we adopted the Weisfeiler–Lehman Neural Machine22 (WLNM) to infer trophic links by learning the organisational characteristics in the substructures surrounding known links in a food web. These examples comprised observed resource to consumer links as positives and sampled directed non-links as negatives, rather than treating every unobserved pair as a confirmed absence. These known links contain be both observed (positive) and absent (negative) links in the empirical data. A neural network is used to perform link prediction by examining whether the substructural pattern of an undetermined link is closer to that of a positive or negative link. The original WLNM was designed for undirected graphs. Here, we modified the method to retain the resource to consumer direction of energy transfer in food webs, where a directed pair i⟶j represents energy moving from resource i to consumer j. In addition, negative samples were chosen randomly from all absent links in the original WLNM, which would include links that are ecologically implausible in our case. We applied realistic assumptions when generating negative links for model training to ensure ecological realism11,23. We first performed link prediction for a small proportion of links and examine the model’s ability to recover these missing links that may be caused by under-sampling in practice. Secondly, we investigated the minimum amount of empirical data would require constructing whole food webs which can be used reliably for bioassessment. This was achieved by reducing the proportion of links used for training until a balance is reached between the training ratio and model’s performance. We evaluated our approach on 290 food webs from a global dataset by referring to a wide range of accuracy metrics. In the case of constructing food webs from reduced data, we compared key food web properties, such as connectance and mean trophic height, between empirical and pseudo webs.

Original: We converted the original WLNM to generate links in food webs from observed data. The basic principle of WLNM is to learn the structural characteristics from a proportion of recorded (positive) and unrecorded (negative) links, whereby the latter is typically any absent links in the network. For a given link, a small subgraph formed around the vertices of the link is extracted and encoded into a fixed-size matrix according to the organisational roles of the nodes within it24. The encoded matrices from the training set are fed into a feed-forward neural network (i.e. a classifier), which uses the matrices to identify local topological features that constitute a positive, as well as a negative link. To perform link prediction between two given nodes, the classifier compares the features extrapolated from then encoded matrix of the substructure formed around them, and determines whether a positive or a negative link should exist22 (Fig. 1, Methods). To facilitate the application of WLNM to our ecological settings, we have made two major modifications. Firstly, food webs were represented as directed resource to consumer energy transfer networks, such that a candidate pair i⟶j denotes energy transfer from resource i to consumer j. The original WLNM was designed for undirected graphs only; therefore, we altered the encoding by retaining the full directed adjacency matrix, rather than collapsing the matrix into an undirected representation, allowing the direction of trophic energy transfer to be preserved (Supplementary Fig. 1). Secondly, the original WLNM uses a naïve strategy to generate negatives whereby randomly sampled unrecorded links are treated equivalently. However, an unobserved pair in a food web can range from an ecologically less plausible non-link to a plausible but unsampled interaction. To reduce this ambiguity, we implemented negative sampling based on trophic roles with hybrid top-up. Species were assigned to basal, intermediate, or top-consumer classes according to whether they acted only as energy sources/resources, only as energy receivers/consumers, or in both roles in the observed directed food web. Preferred negative examples were then sampled from directed non-links matching one of five trophic-role combinations: top consumer ⟶ top consumer, basal ⟶ basal, top consumer ⟶ basal, top consumer ⟶ intermediate, and intermediate ⟶ basal. If this restricted pool did not contain enough candidates to preserve the two negative per positive sampling ratio, all restricted candidates were retained and only the remaining deficit was completed using random valid directed non-links. With the expanded five constraint definition, 207 of the 290 food webs had a sufficient restricted pool, while 83 required the hybrid top-up procedure (Methods, Supplementary Fig. 2). As of the original study the size of the subgraphs is fixed at 10 nodes22 (Methods).

Original: Across the 290 food webs, the model showed a conservative error profile, producing high precision and very few false positive links while recovering a moderate proportion of withheld trophic links. In the food web illustrated in Fig. 2, across 50 runs at the 90% training ratio, the model recovered on average 38.8 true positive links and generated only 0.6 false positives, while leaving 38.2 withheld observed links unrecovered as false negatives and correctly identifying 153.4 true negatives. The corresponding metric values were ROC-AUC = 0.971, PR-AUC = 0.585, F1 = 0.664, MCC = 0.626, precision = 0.985, recall = 0.504 and TSS = 0.501. This indicates that most predicted links were reliable and that the model generated very few false positives, but recall was moderate, so some withheld observed links were not recovered. The few false positives should therefore be interpreted cautiously, as several may correspond to ecologically plausible but unrecorded interactions under the resource to consumer energy-transfer convention. We found that our approach is accurate in identifying majority of the holdout interactions that have been omitted in the training, achieving a number of high true positive predictions (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1). The number of false negatives which are holdout links that have been missed by the model (i.e. false negatives) is very low. In addition, the number of links that did not exist but were generated by the model (i.e. false positives) is also extremely low. However, it is worth noting that many of these false positive links appear to be logical in the ecological context, as they are typically within the existing diet range of a consumer (Fig. 2), which could potentially represent interactions that may have been missed in the original dataset11.

The updated model has a conservative error profile: high precision, low false-positive rate, moderate recall and improved balanced performance in MCC and TSS. Previous studies based on random forest and a stacked model that uses both species attributes and structural information reported comparable model performance (TSS = 0.53-0.7723, and ROC-AUC = 0.95 ± 0.06 and PR-AUC = 0.68 ± 0.2025 respectively), but their evaluations are restricted to the very limited metrics that are reported here only, unlike the comprehensive sets of metrics we have illustrated here. Moreover, metrics, such as ROC-AUC, have been found to be uninformative in the context of ecology. This is due to the fact that food webs are usually sparse with a connectance of about 20%, which means correct predictions on a larger number of negative links would disproportionally over-estimate the overall performance11.

Original: We investigated how well our model is able to construct whole food webs from limited data. To achieve this, we varied the training ratio from 10% to 90% of the observed trophic links with an increment of 10%. At each training ratio, the selected proportion of observed links was used as positive training data, while the remaining observed links were withheld for evaluation. For each training ratio and food web, negative examples were sampled using the same negative-sampling procedure based on trophic roles with hybrid top-up, preserving the two negative per positive ratio while prioritising ecologically informed directed non-links whenever available. The model was then trained and evaluated separately for each food web and training ratio. This procedure was repeated 50 times per food web, and scores were averaged within each food web. Performance increased strongly from 10% to approximately 40–60% training data and then largely plateaued (Fig. 4). The clearest improvements from 10% to 90% training data were observed for ROC-AUC (0.733 to 0.874), precision (0.662 to 0.889), MCC (0.393 to 0.615) and TSS (0.344 to 0.541), whereas recall increased more moderately (0.432 to 0.579) and PR-AUC remained comparatively stable. Because the largest gains occurred before 60%, we evaluated whether pseudo-webs reconstructed from 60% training data reproduced empirical food-web properties. After Tukey outlier filtering, pseudo-webs broadly reproduced empirical network structure, but with systematic deviations: connectance was slightly lower than in empirical webs (-11.30%), mean trophic height was slightly higher (+5.40%), and both mean generality and mean vulnerability were lower (-7.33% each) (Fig. 5). Original: Global environmental change alters species traits such as body size and metabolic rate, and by extension, population biomasses and trophic positions in food webs27,28.  This results in trophic links between species varying with environmental conditions, and across space and time1,3. While we are yet to fully understand the interplay among environmental stressors, species traits and the complex interactions in ecosystems, machine learning can provide a powerful tool to decipher the underlying principles that govern trophic link assembly, particularly when the quantity and resolution of food web data is increasing exponentially. Here, we have demonstrated how the previously unexplored richness in the organisational patterns of food web substructure can be automatically retrieved by the WLNM technique without any prior assumptions22. We made two main modifications to WLNM to ensure the model suit our ecological application. Firstly, unlike the original model, links are encoded so that the resource to consumer energy-transfer direction is preserved, clearly distinguishing the role of an energy source from that of an energy receiver. Secondly, rather than treating all unobserved directed pairs as equivalent negatives, we prioritised more reliable negative examples using negative sampling based on trophic roles and applied a hybrid random top-up only when the restricted pool was insufficient11. We evaluated our model’s ability to perform link prediction whereby 90% of the observed data is used for training, and found that the model is accurate in recovering the 10% holdout links with high precision and TSS scores, and low error rate. In addition, unlike other link prediction methods4, our model is not sensitive to food web size and connectance. Furthermore, our approach can be utilised to construct whole food webs with realistic food web properties using as little as 60% of the original trophic links, demonstrating the enormous scope for using machine learning techniques to capitalise on existing food web data and developing novel ways for web construction11.
